analysis.one_liner: Gives public employees federal collective bargaining rights where state law falls short.
analysis.headline: Despite 229 cosponsors — including three Republicans — the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Labor Relations Authority to check whether each state's laws give public workers real collective bargaining rights. In states that fall short, the federal agency would set up and run union elections, good-faith bargaining, written contracts, and binding arbitration for public employees. It also bans strikes or lockouts that would disrupt emergency or public safety services.
analysis.who_benefits: Public employees — teachers, nurses, first responders, transit workers, and others — in states whose laws fall short of federal minimum bargaining rights would gain the right to organize, elect a union, and bargain over wages and working conditions, with binding arbitration to settle deadlocked contracts and a private right of action to enforce the rights in court. Labor unions gain members and dues in roughly half the states where public-sector bargaining is weak or banned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public employees in states without union rights

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal floor of collective bargaining rights for public employees — the right to organize, join or decline to join a union, bargain through representatives of their own choosing, and act together — in any state whose laws do not already match the standard.

Requires public employers to recognize a union chosen by majority vote, bargain in good faith, and put any agreement in a written contract, with grievance procedures ending in binding arbitration when bargaining deadlocks.
Gives workers enforcement teeth: the Federal Labor Relations Authority can order compliance, and after 180 days an unpaid charge can go straight to federal court, with attorneys' fees available.
Lets employees pay union dues through payroll deduction if they individually authorize it, a right several states currently bar.
Bans strikes, lockouts, and job actions that would measurably disrupt emergency or public safety services, and leaves stricter state strike laws in place.
Respects state arrangements that already meet the standard, exempts small towns under 5,000 people or 25 employees if the state opts them out, and preserves existing contracts and bargaining units.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately their taxpayers, would bear the cost: higher public-sector labor costs from binding arbitration, compliance with Federal Labor Relations Authority rules, and the loss of some state control over their own workforce rules. States that already met the standard would owe little.

drawbacks.text: It overrides state choices: about half the states have deliberately limited or barred public-sector bargaining, and the bill replaces their rules with a federal regime run by an agency created for the federal workforce.
Binding arbitration is a real cost for local budgets — an arbitrator's contract award can bind a city or school district even when elected officials judge the community cannot afford it.
The costs fall on state and local taxpayers, who fund public payrolls, with no dedicated funding source in the bill beyond an open-ended appropriation.

Bargaining rights for police unions in particular have been used to negotiate protections that make officer discipline harder — a consequence supporters of the bill had to accept, though the bill does leave stricter state laws in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains to workers are substantial: about half of states provide little or no collective bargaining for public employees, and this bill would have given those workers a federal backstop with real enforcement, while barring service-disrupting strikes in safety fields. The costs are also real — higher public payrolls and arbitration awards funded by taxpayers, and a serious loss of state control over employment policy. On balance the trade favors working people, but the one-sided federal override and binding arbitration are genuine costs an honest supporter would have to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and was never given a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 25, 2019 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
It drew 229 cosponsors — 226 of the 231 House Democrats and 3 of the 197 House Republicans.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public employers and state governments that would have faced federal collective bargaining mandates are better off, since the bill never advanced. Public employees in weak-bargaining states gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 25, 2019 and assembled 228 original cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Robert Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never scheduled it for a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote; the action history shows no activity after the June 25, 2019 referral.

sides.party_line_note: 226 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored, versus only 3 of 197 House Republicans, making this an almost entirely one-party bill.

industries.note: The bill would let unions organize public employees in the roughly half of states where bargaining rights are weak or absent, adding members and dues revenue. Its interest here runs alongside the workers it would represent.

Public employers would face mandatory recognition of unions, good-faith bargaining, and binding arbitration that can override their budget decisions. Their gain from the bill's failure is lower labor costs and retained control over their workforce.
